speaker: Percy Liang
title: No Priors Ep. 7 | With Stanford Professor Dr. Percy Liang
question: In foundation model research on complex reasoning and planning, why is simply scaling models on relevant training data insufficient?
guest: To a first-order approximation, larger models trained on the relevant data seem to do well on various benchmarks. I think maybe there isn't enough emphasis on data efficiency and how quickly and robustly you can get to these points, because it has been well documented that benchmarks can be gameable. So even though you do well on a benchmark doesn't mean you've necessarily solved the problem—one has to be a little bit cautious about that. Obviously, scale and more data is one clear direction, but in terms of orthogonal directions, several things have to happen. One is the ability to handle greater context lengths. If you think about a long reasoning chain, transformers are fixed, and while there are ways to extend them, fundamentally it's a fixed model. Then there's advanced problem-solving: if you want to solve a math problem or prove something, the language model thinks out a chain of thought and generates token by token. But we know that when humans solve a problem, you try different things, you backtrack—it's much more flexible, iterative, and can last a lot longer than a few iterations. What architecture can handle that level of complexity is still an outstanding question.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Scaling on relevant data mostly improves a model's ability to reproduce patterns it has seen, not its ability to carry out the underlying reasoning procedure. Several lines of research point to the same gap.

Models trained this way tend to learn statistical shortcuts rather than general algorithms, so performance collapses when problems are longer, deeper or structured differently from the training distribution. Work on compositional tasks (for example, multi-digit multiplication and puzzle solving) shows accuracy falling sharply as the number of reasoning steps grows, even with abundant in-distribution training data.

The architecture is also part of the problem. Autoregressive generation commits to one token at a time with no built-in mechanism for lookahead, backtracking or checking a partial plan against a goal, and per-step errors compound over long chains. Planning requires searching a combinatorially large space, which no feasible dataset can cover by example.

Finally, the training objective rewards plausible continuations, not verified correctness or an accurate world model of how actions change state.

That is why research pairs scaling with other ingredients: explicit search, external verifiers and tools, world models, and training methods that reward correct reasoning.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Simply scaling model parameters and training data is insufficient because passive imitation on static datasets optimizes for statistical pattern matching rather than deliberative problem-solving. Models trained via standard supervised or next-token objectives frequently learn brittle shortcuts and surface correlations instead of generalizable causal rules or accurate world models, causing performance to degrade sharply on out-of-distribution or compositionally novel tasks. Furthermore, training corpora typically record polished final solutions rather than the underlying search process—the dead ends, constraint checks, and revisions required to discover them. Architecturally, standard autoregressive inference commits to outputs sequentially with fixed compute per step, lacking explicit lookahead or backtracking; over long planning horizons, small per-step errors compound exponentially and derail execution. Because complex combinatorial reasoning demands adaptive computation that cannot be memorized or compressed into fixed-compute forward passes, reliable planning requires mechanisms beyond pretraining scale, including reinforcement learning, explicit verification or environment feedback, and inference-time search to dynamically evaluate alternatives and self-correct.

noweb.answer: Simply scaling model parameters and static training data fails to solve complex reasoning and planning because next-token prediction fundamentally differs from deliberative search. Standard autoregressive architectures allocate fixed compute per token and commit sequentially to outputs without native mechanisms for lookahead, state verification, or backtracking, causing small per-step errors to compound exponentially over long horizons. Furthermore, static corpora predominantly record polished final solutions rather than the latent trial-and-error, dead ends, and self-correction trajectories that produce valid plans. Consequently, larger models often rely on memorized templates and surface shortcuts instead of learning generalizable algorithms or causal world models, leading to brittle performance on novel constraints and out-of-distribution problems. High-quality multi-step reasoning data is also finite, creating a bottleneck that passive imitation cannot overcome. Achieving robust reasoning and planning therefore requires moving beyond pretraining scale by integrating adaptive test-time compute, explicit search, external verifiers, and reinforcement learning with grounded feedback so models can actively explore, evaluate, and revise multi-step decisions.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Scaling helps, but on its own it doesn't produce reliable reasoning or planning, for a few reasons. Complex reasoning means searching very large combinatorial spaces, such as possible proof steps, program edits or action sequences, and the training data can never cover enough of that space for pattern-matching to stand in for search. Models trained to predict the next token learn statistical regularities, but planning needs systematic, compositional generalization: recombining known rules in new ways, often over long horizons. Scaled-up models still tend to fail on that, especially on problems longer or deeper than the ones they were trained on.

The feedback is also sparse and delayed. Whether a plan or proof works is usually only clear at the end, so imitating example solutions doesn't teach the model to explore, backtrack, or check intermediate steps. Reasoning also needs internal consistency and verifiable correctness, while sampling from probabilities lets small errors compound. Finally, good data on the reasoning process itself, not just final answers, is scarce.

Researchers such as Bommasani et al. (2021) therefore argue for adding search, planning algorithms, tool use, verifiers, and reinforcement or interactive learning on top of scale.

Standard autoregressive models allocate fixed compute per token and generate outputs left-to-right without native lookahead, backtracking, or verification. As planning horizons grow, minor early mistakes compound rapidly, and the combinatorial explosion of possible state transitions ensures that training corpora can never cover all novel compositions, causing brittle generalization to longer or out-of-distribution problems. Moreover, natural training data rarely captures the intermediate process of exploring dead ends, testing hypotheses, and recovering from errors; imitating only final solutions teaches heuristic shortcuts rather than reliable constraint satisfaction. Consequently, achieving robust reasoning and planning requires moving beyond pretraining scale alone toward methods that explicitly support search, verification, and adaptive inference-time computation, such as reinforcement learning with verifiable feedback and integration with external tools or world models.

noweb.answer: Simply scaling models on relevant training data is insufficient for complex reasoning and planning because standard autoregressive training optimizes statistical pattern matching rather than systematic problem solving. First, the space of multi-step reasoning chains and long-horizon plans grows combinatorially, making it impossible for static training datasets to cover every novel composition or edge case; models that rely on memorizing or interpolating seen trajectories break down out of distribution. Second, standard next-token prediction allocates a fixed amount of computation per token and commits sequentially without native mechanisms to look ahead, verify intermediate steps, or backtrack. As a result, a single early mistake compounds across subsequent steps into an invalid plan. Finally, imitating static solution traces teaches surface plausibility rather than causal validity or goal optimality. Achieving reliable reasoning and planning therefore requires going beyond training-data scaling to incorporate test-time compute, explicit search and backtracking, self-verification, and reinforcement learning from verifiable outcomes or interactive environment feedback.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Scaling on relevant data improves a model’s ability to recognize familiar patterns, but complex reasoning and planning require it to combine those patterns in situations it has never seen. The number of possible combinations grows rapidly with the length of a problem, so training data can cover only a fraction of them. Small errors can also compound: one invalid deduction or action can derail an otherwise plausible solution.

Standard next-token training rewards predicting what comes next in an example. It gives the model no direct incentive to check whether each step follows from the premises or whether a sequence of actions actually achieves the goal. That is why scaling can help while still leaving a role for training with feedback on intermediate steps and for methods that let the model search, verify, and revise its reasoning at inference time.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Scaling models on relevant examples can improve reasoning, but a correct answer alone gives little feedback about which steps made it correct. A model can learn a shortcut that works on familiar problems and fails when a new problem combines familiar elements in an unfamiliar way. Planning adds another difficulty: an early choice can look sensible even when it makes the goal unreachable several steps later.

More data can reduce these failures, but it does not guarantee that a model will explore alternatives, track the consequences of its choices, or revise a flawed plan. Training on intermediate steps or outcomes can give the model better feedback, while search and verification can help it test a proposed solution before committing to it.
